doc: Typed local persistence for canonical display-capture artifacts. Each physical storage record contains either one complete [`DisplayCaptureArtifact`] or one [`PresentationOutputArtifact`](crate::presentation_output::PresentationOutputArtifact) that embeds a display artifact, composition timing, and before/after output topology. The storage record parent orders physical appends; the embedded [`crate::display::DisplayReceiptV2`] parent independently orders display observations across both record kinds. Opening or recovering a journal replays and checks both chains before exposing any writable state. A successful append proves only that the exact typed candidate passed before I/O, `File::sync_all` returned success, and the appended carrier bytes were reread through the retained handle and matched that candidate before its semantic head was published. doc: Exclusive-writer filesystem journal for canonical storage records. The journal is deliberately narrower than a database. On Windows it retains one read/write handle opened with sharing disabled, appends one fully encoded [`StorageRecord`] at the verified end of file, calls [`std::fs::File::sync_all`], and only then publishes the new local head. Recovery admits the longest canonical parent-linked prefix and exposes the entire rejected suffix. It never truncates, skips, or resynchronizes automatically. A successful sync is evidence that the operating-system call returned success. It is not an atomic-append, power-loss, rollback-resistance, custody, availability, or consensus proof.

doc: Canonical outcome of one deterministic fixed simulation tick. A [`TickOutcome`] commits the exact consumed control batch, the ordered disposition of every edit attempt, the pre/post world and coordinate-history heads, the post-tick camera state, and any game/composite frame pair produced by that tick. It deliberately excludes presentation receipts and display capture: those occur later and may point back to this outcome without forming a dependency cycle. The tag proves byte identity under SHA-256. Full validity additionally requires resolving the parent, replaying the declared `bitblock/tick-outcome/v3` transition, checking the fixed genesis camera for tick zero, and independently verifying referenced frame objects.

doc: bbmutate.py -- measure whether the test suite would actually notice. python tools/bbmutate.py # every module with a canonical encoder python tools/bbmutate.py frame tick # just these A green suite proves nothing on its own; it has to be shown *failing* for the change you care about. This crate's whole claim is byte-exact canonical encodings, so the change worth measuring is a canonical byte moving. The mutation is surgical: every `to_be_bytes()` in one module's production scope becomes `to_le_bytes()`. That is exactly a byte-order change inside the hashed domain and nothing else -- no behaviour, no error text, no control flow. If a module's tests pin its canonical bytes, this must fail them. If it survives, the suite does not pin that module's encoding and a refactor there is unguarded. Whole-module rather than per-site, deliberately: the question is "does anything notice this module's bytes changing", not which line is best covered. It also sidesteps a false blind spot -- `u8::to_be_bytes` and `to_le_bytes` are the same single byte, so a one-site run on a u8 would survive while proving nothing. Local only, never CI. It rewrites files and restores them from git, so the tree must be clean before it runs.

doc: bbtime.py -- measure where verification time actually goes, per test and per module. python tools/bbtime.py # serial and accurate; writes target/bbtiming.json python tools/bbtime.py --best-of-3 # three samples per test, keep the fastest python tools/bbtime.py --parallel # rough sweep only; see the warning below python tools/bbtime.py --top 30 # show more rows python tools/bbtime.py --build # what it costs to touch each module The point is that bottlenecks should surface themselves rather than be guessed at. Every previous speedup in this repository came from measuring and finding the cost somewhere other than where it looked: the index's 18s was a per-item regex sweep and not the obvious string joining, and the full tier's 8s was a single test hashing a 27MB executable six times. Time is attributed to the module that owns the test, so it lands on the same nodes `bbgraph dag` already ranks. That answers a question neither tool can alone: `protocol` is reached by 29 of 33 modules, and now its verification cost is a number rather than an intuition. The output is written to target/ rather than index/, deliberately. It is a measurement of this machine on this day -- it would differ on every host, and index/ has to regenerate byte-identically from the tree. **On the numbers.** Each test runs in its own process with `--test-threads 1`, and process start is measured and subtracted. `--parallel` is a rough sweep and its **ranking is not trustworthy**. Eight concurrent children, each opening a full libtest thread pool, oversubscribe the machine badly enough to reorder the results: against best-of-three isolated runs, a 0.04s test was reported at 3.88s and ranked slowest of all, while a genuinely 1.93s test came fourth. That was measured, not feared, and it is why serial is the default. Serial numbers are still wall-clock samples rather than a benchmark. Take a difference under about 20% between two rows as noise, and use `--best-of-3` when a specific pair matters. **Per-test isolation double-counts anything a process pays once.** The executable fingerprint is memoised per process, so in a real run the 27MB hash happens once for all 53 bin tests; here every test that touches it pays again. Isolated cost answers "what does this test cost alone", not "what would deleting it save". **The sum is not the wall clock.** ~30s of measured test cost becomes ~3.5s of tier, because the binaries run concurrently and libtest parallelises within each. What sets the floor is the slowest single binary, and inside that, its slowest test. Optimise the longest pole, never the largest sum.
name: bbtime
summary: bbtime.py -- measure where verification time actually goes, per test and per module.

doc: bbverify.py -- one command that says whether anything broke. python tools/bbverify.py quick # per edit python tools/bbverify.py full # per commit (default) python tools/bbverify.py full --force # ignore the cache and run everything python tools/bbverify.py list # what each check reads, and why The point of a refactor gate here is narrow and unusual: this crate's value is byte-exact canonical encodings, so "nothing broke" means *no canonical byte moved*. 101 literal content tags are asserted across the test suite and 24 Python suites reconstruct those same payloads without importing any Rust. A refactor that changes a byte fails both, from opposite directions. `tools/bbmutate.py` measures whether that is true rather than assuming it: 25 of 25 modules fail when a canonical byte order is flipped. Two tiers, because they detect different things at different speeds. **quick** is the Rust tests plus clippy. This is what actually catches a moved byte: the literal tag assertions live inside the Rust tests, so they run here. **full** adds the independent Python vectors, `cargo fmt`, the metric registry audit, and the index gates. The vector suites execute no Rust at all -- they derive the expected digests from the schema -- so they cannot detect a Rust change on their own. What they detect is the two implementations *disagreeing*, which is why they belong to the per-commit tier rather than the inner loop. Both tiers run `--workspace`: without it cargo tests only the root package, and after the workspace split that was 43 tests of 397 with every gate still green. `full` adds `--features protocol-research`, which is also what CI now runs. How many tests ran is therefore a gate of its own -- see EXPECTED_TESTS. Three things make it fast, in the order they matter. **Every check declares what it reads.** Editing `docs/PROTOCOL.md` cannot change what `cargo test` does, so a check whose inputs are byte-identical to the last run that passed is skipped rather than repeated. This is the same content-addressing the crate itself is built on: the inputs are hashed, and an unchanged digest means the answer is already known. It is also why the checks are declarative records rather than a script -- the input set is the interesting half. **One build, then everything at once.** `cargo test` compiles three test binaries and walks them one after another -- 2.5s + 2.6s + 2.3s of mostly idle CPU on a sixteen-core machine. `cargo test --no-run` costs 0.4s warm and reports where those binaries are, so they run concurrently, with clippy and the Python work alongside. A tier costs its slowest single job instead of the sum. **The cache is conservative.** It records only checks that passed, it keys on this file's own bytes as well as the subject's, and anything it cannot read makes it run rather than skip. A stale skip would be a silent false green, which is worse than any amount of waiting. Every stage here has been watched failing before being trusted, per docs/TIMELINES.md: "a check that has not been watched failing is not yet enforcement".

doc: Independent stdlib vectors for coordinate key order and authenticated node arity. `docs/AUTHENTICATED_STATE_PLAN.md` retains an undecided question this file measures rather than argues: whether a future spatial/chunk/Morton key profile is worth a migration, or whether point and multiproofs under plain ``x || y || z`` suffice. It reduces to counting. A sparse authenticated multiproof over the fixed 192-bit keyspace must carry, for every node on the union of the queried root-to-leaf paths, each child of that node that is not itself on the union. Children whose subtree holds no world coordinate are the well-known empty-subtree constants and cost a bitmap bit rather than a hash, so only NON-EMPTY children are counted as carried material. TWO DECISIONS, TWO METRICS, AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME. * Candidates A and B are both BINARY hash trees. Their carried material is the non-empty sibling count measured here, so this file speaks directly to them. * A later Verkle lane would carry roughly one commitment per LEVEL, with an aggregated opening, and the sibling count would not appear in its proof. Node arity is therefore a Verkle-lane variable that this file does not price. The structural table below reports only which arities can tile the key and which align with a cubic chunk; it is not a proof-size comparison for that lane. WHAT THIS FILE ESTABLISHES. Exact carried-sibling counts for the named finite fixtures below. Nothing else. It is not a security argument, not an implementation, not a selection between Candidate A and Candidate B, and not a Verkle admission. It does not import or launch Bitblock and does not read or write repository state. WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT MODEL. Node encoding overhead, Patricia path compression (which carries strictly less than the sparse bound counted here), proof system constants, prover and verifier time, storage layout, and cache behaviour. Run: python -B tools/key_profile_vectors.py

summary: Independent stdlib vectors for coordinate key order and authenticated node arity.
